newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Campaign to save underwater Alexandria gathers pace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Campaign to save underwater Alexandria gathers pace.

text.p: A campaign to save the submerged remains of ancient Alexandria has scored its first victories on the strength of persuasive evidence that archaeologists have found Cleopatra's palace under the harbour.

The site of the palace, scene of the drama between Cleopatra, Mark Antony and the Caesars in the dying days of Pharaonic Egypt, seems to be on the seabed just a stone's throw from the heart of the modern city, archaeologists say.
The sea protected it from pillage after earthquakes changed the coastline but in the 20th century new enemies, especially sewage and harbour works, pose a threat to its survival.

The governor of Alexandria, now a busy port of more than three million people, has promised for a start to stop pumping the raw sewage into the harbour, where parts of the old city lie under five to six metres (17 to 20 feet) of filthy water.

"They have already stopped in some places and they say that by the end of this year it will stop completely," said Ibrahinm Darwish, the head of a new underwater archaeology department at the state's Supreme Council for Antiquities.
DRAIN THE WHOLE HARBOUR
"Sometimes we cannot see more than 15 cms (six inches) under the water so we have to stop working," said underwater cameraman Roland Savoye, member of a French archaeological team.

The armed forces, bowing to a clamour of protest from archaeologists and local societies, have suspended for the moment the practice of throwing concrete blocks into the water to protect their military installations from erosion.
"They have given us two months to survey the area to check for archaeological sites. Now we are trying to stop this practice once and for all," Darwish said.
The next step, advocated by a broad coalition of local activists, will be to move the army off one side of the eastern harbour and declare a protected archaeological area.
The Archaeological Society of Alexandria has sent an appeal on the subject to Suzanne Mubarak, the wife of President Hosni Mubarak, and to Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri and others.

Ali Hassan, head of the state's Supreme Council for Antiquities, says the authorities are seriously considering an ambitious plan to drain the whole harbour, about three square km (1.2 square miles), so that excavation can proceed on dry land.

Others, smelling profit, want an "underwater archaeological park" where foreign scuba divers would pay large sums of money for a ticket to swim among the granite columns, sphinxes and Greek statuary which adorned the ancient walkways.
DIVERS FOCUS ON ISLAND

The impetus for the sudden interest in the area is the work of two French underwater archaeologists, Jean Yves Empereur and Franck Goddio, who have used new technologies to map the ancient objects which litter the seabed.
Empereur's divers have been salvaging antiquities from around the probable site of the ancient Pharos, or lighthouse, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.

Goddio, president of the European Institute of Marine Archaeology in Paris, has worked on the sunken royal quarter to the east, trying to match ancient descriptions of the city with the features they can identify under the water.
Using the satellite-based Global Positioning System, his team has fixed to within 30 cm (one foot) the location of more than 1,000 artifacts and architectural features.
They resumed this year's surveying on June 2, concentrating on the probable site of Antirrhodos island, where the Greek geographer Strabo says Cleopatra had her palace.
Their work is generating so much new material that old theories are under threat and the whole world of Alexandrian archaeology is in turmoil with speculative alternatives.
OLD DEBATES REVIVED
Fawzi Fakhrani, doyen of Greco-Roman archaeologists in Alexandria, said last month he was convinced Goddio's divers have correctly identified the palace.
"It's for sure," he told a seminar. "He has found not only the palace of Cleopatra but everything that Strabo described."

Fakhrani's main argument is that the paving stones on Antirrhodos have grey mortar, not the red mortar introduced under Augustus, the Roman emperor who in 30 BC overthrew Cleopatra's family and incorporated Egypt into his empire.
But Darwish is much more cautious. "We cannot say we have found the palace because we have no proof. Excavation continues and when we have proof we will announce it," he said.
Other old debates have won a new lease of life. Was there, for example, a large settlement in the Alexandria area before Alexander the Great ordered the city built in 332 BC?
Why are some of the antiquities found near the lighthouse about 1,000 years older than the city itself?
With waters free of sewage and legal protection for the site, the archaeologists might produce some of the answers.
